In this VladTV interview, John Franzese Jr. reflects on growing up in Rockville Centre, Long Island, as the son of Colombo crime family underboss Sonny Franzese and younger brother of Michael Franzese. Speaking with Vlad, John recalls his father’s 1966 homicide trial in the killing of Ernest “The Hawk,” explaining how an inmate’s courtroom claim helped Sonny beat the murder case. He also revisits the bank robbery charges, a 43-count gambling indictment, and the 1970 sentence that sent Sonny Franzese to prison for 50 years when John was just 10 years old.

John also opens up about the emotional impact of losing his father to the federal system, the family’s belief that Sonny was framed, and what home life was like behind the Mafia image—including fear, discipline, and violence inside the household. Plus, he shares a private off-camera reunion with music executive Steve Rifkind after decades apart.

In this VladTV interview, Marlow Bates reflects on Baltimore street life, prison, drug money disputes, and the violence that followed when people crossed the line. Pressed by Vlad for court-exposed examples, Bates discusses how conflicts over drugs and cash were enforced through beatings and stabbings, while avoiding details tied to murder allegations due to legal risks. He recalls past murder charges he says he beat in court, references a disputed ballistic expert named Joseph, and describes long-running tension with law enforcement.

Bates also shares a vivid story about confronting a childhood bully named Ducky, while Timmirror adds perspective on keeping a low profile during the drug era, running a construction company, and handling large amounts of cash. The conversation touches on Baltimore crime history, street politics, prison stories, dirty money, and the harsh realities behind the drug trade.

In this VladTV interview, Tito “TJ” Dominguez recounts a dangerous trip to Colombia after a cocaine deal left him owed roughly $3–5 million. Dominguez explains the underworld logic he learned from figures like Luis, including how reputation, fear, and accountability shaped decisions in the drug trade. He describes arriving quietly, paying hotel staff for information, hiring a cab driver named Angel, and setting up surveillance on the debtor’s home while avoiding attention from powerful Colombian connections tied to Pablo Escobar and Gustavo Gaviria.

The story builds to a tense standoff outside a guarded mansion, where Dominguez says he blocked the gate until the man agreed to talk. He also details how part of the repayment came through a Ferrari dealership in California, underscoring the unusual ways drug money moved across borders. A candid look at cocaine trafficking, Colombia, organized crime, and survival in a violent era.

Terrance “Gangsta” Williams returns to VladTV to break down the long-awaited Cash Money and No Limit reunion tour, sharing why he wasn’t surprised Birdman, Slim and Master P finally found common ground. Williams explains how the tour could benefit B.G., Juvenile and Mannie Fresh, while reflecting on his own role in the early Cash Money family.

The conversation digs into the historic New Orleans tension between Cash Money Records and No Limit Records, including Master P’s Priority Records run, Cash Money’s Universal deal, the Hot Boys name dispute, and the 2000 No Limit film *Hot Boyz* starring Snoop Dogg and Silkk the Shocker. Williams also reacts to the viral Verzuz handshake between Birdman and Master P, questions its sincerity, and recalls how street ties, prison politics, and regional loyalty shaped the rivalry. A candid look at Southern hip-hop history from someone who lived it.

Charleston White joins VladTV for a pointed conversation about Young Thug editing an album verse to remove a shoutout to Israel amid the ongoing Israel-Palestine debate. Vlad questions the move, noting that Jewish attorney Brian Steel stood by Young Thug during one of the most serious moments of his legal battle, even spending time in custody while working on the case. The discussion also touches on music executive Lyor Cohen’s support of Thug, past connections to rabbis and Israel, and how public pressure can influence artists’ political choices.

White adds his perspective on trends, antisemitism, Palestinian support, and why changing lyrics can make an artist appear more political rather than less. The interview explores hip-hop, celebrity accountability, the YSL case fallout, social media reactions, and the complicated intersection of rap culture, religion, and global politics.

In this VladTV interview, former Mexican Mafia member Rene “Boxer” Enriquez reflects on his 1988 parole, returning to California streets after prison, and the harsh reality of trying to enforce La Eme authority outside the walls. Enriquez discusses Artesia 13, Boyle Heights, White Fence, drug dealer “taxing,” and encounters with figures including Raymond Shrier, Rock Luna, Jesse Moreno, Jesse Aragon, David Galvan “Big Spider,” Little Maurice, and Jocko.

The conversation turns to Cynthia Gordon, a mother of two connected to a Mexican Mafia member, who Enriquez says was killed in 1989 after accusations of missing drug money from a controlled dope house. Speaking with Vlad, Enriquez accepts responsibility for ordering her death and says no explanation can justify taking her life, admitting she should have simply been removed from the situation.
